messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 36

She is 52, married, and has spent most of her adult life organizing chaos into workable plans. As a project manager, she is used to deadlines, competing priorities, and the pressure of keeping people aligned when they are moving in different directions. Before the trauma, she prides herself on being steady. Family members describe her as the one who remembers appointments, notices details others miss, and stays composed in a crisis.

The event that changes her begins on an ordinary day that now feels unreal in its normalcy. She is in a public place in her Middle Eastern community when a terrorist attack unfolds nearby. At first, she does not understand what she is hearing. There is a sharp noise, then a second one, then the terrible recognition in the faces around her. People start running. She remembers the sound of screaming more vividly than anything else, and the way her own body seems to lag behind her mind, as if she is watching herself from a distance. In the confusion she is separated from others, and for a few minutes she is certain she will die. She later describes those minutes as suspended, crowded with images she cannot shut off: the ground, blood, a dropped shoe, someone calling for a mother.

In the days afterward, she functions because she has to. Her husband wants her to rest, but she cannot sit still for long. She checks doors and windows repeatedly and listens for every sound outside. She keeps the television off because any breaking news alert makes her stomach clench. She tries to return to work quickly, telling herself that she is “fine enough,” but at her desk she loses track of simple tasks and has to reread emails several times. Meetings that once felt manageable now leave her tense and distracted, and she notices she is sitting nearer the door, scanning the room, tracking who comes and goes. She begins to avoid the part of town where the attack occurred, then avoids crowded spaces more generally. Even grocery stores become difficult when the aisles are full and she cannot see an easy exit.

Sleep changes early and stays changed. She falls asleep exhausted, then wakes suddenly in the night with her heart racing, disoriented and sure for a few seconds that danger is near. Sometimes she wakes from dreams that replay fragments of the attack without warning. In the morning she feels as though she has been bracing all night. Her body stays tight, shoulders raised, jaw clenched, and she notices how easily she startles at a slammed car door or a loud laugh behind her. Her husband says she seems “far away” at times, and he is right; there are stretches when she is present only in pieces, going through routine actions while feeling detached from herself and from the life around her.

What troubles her most is the way ordinary reminders intrude. A siren on the street, a sudden crowd near a building entrance, even a news image from another country can pull her right back into that moment of terror. She feels anger when people speak casually about violence, and then guilt for feeling angry when she knows others have suffered more. As a Middle Eastern woman, she also carries a private layer of fear and shame about how her community is viewed, and after the attack she becomes more guarded in public. She watches faces for signs of suspicion. She speaks less in meetings when conversations turn to politics or security. At times she worries that her own fear makes her seem weak, especially because she has built a career on being reliable and in control.

Over time she has not fallen apart, but she has become narrower in how she moves through the world. She still works, still manages projects, still cares for her family, yet each day requires more effort than it used to. She is aware that she is living around the edges of what happened, always aware of exits, noises, and the possibility that a normal moment could change without warning.
